dietary-supplement.short: A product taken on top of normal food: pills, powders, drinks, gels. It may fix a shortfall, give convenient energy, or aim to improve performance or health.

ergogenic-aid.short: Anything taken or done to improve physical performance directly. 'Ergogenic' means 'work-making'.

caffeine.short: A stimulant in coffee, tea, cola, gels and pills. It acts mainly on the brain, so effort feels easier. One of the few supplements with good evidence.

dietary-nitrate.short: A small ion found in leafy greens and beetroot. The body can turn it into nitric oxide. Concentrated beetroot juice is the usual supplement.

food-first.short: The rule that an athlete gets the everyday diet right before using supplements, and adds one only for a clear, tested need.

supplement-contamination.short: A substance in a supplement that isn't on its label, such as a banned steroid or stimulant, from poor manufacturing or deliberate adding.

anti-doping-rule-violation.short: Breaking the anti-doping rules, e.g. a banned substance found in a urine sample. It can bring a ban even when the substance came, unknowingly, from a contaminated supplement.

third-party-testing.short: An independent lab tests batches of a product for banned substances, so athletes can pick lower-risk products. It lowers the risk but can't remove it.

adenosine.short: A molecule that builds up in the brain and binds its receptors, damping down nerve signalling, so you feel tired. Caffeine blocks those receptors.

cyp1a2.short: The liver enzyme that breaks down over 95% of caffeine. A common polymorphism in its gene is thought to make people faster or slower at clearing caffeine.

nitrite.short: The middle step between nitrate and nitric oxide. Bacteria on the tongue make it from the nitrate in saliva.

sodium-bicarbonate.short: Baking soda (NaHCO₃). Taken a few hours before a hard effort, it raises the blood's bicarbonate buffer, so more acid can leave the working muscle.

beta-alanine.short: An amino acid the muscle needs to make carnosine. Taken daily for weeks, it raises the carnosine in the muscle.

carnosine.short: A small molecule inside muscle fibres that soaks up H⁺: a buffer within the muscle itself.

alkalosis.short: A rise in pH (fewer free H⁺) in blood or muscle: the opposite of acidosis. Sodium bicarbonate causes a mild alkalosis in the blood.

paraesthesia.short: Harmless pins-and-needles tingling of the skin: the known side effect of large single doses of beta-alanine.

creatine-monohydrate.short: The usual form of creatine supplement. It raises the muscle's creatine and PCr stores by about 20–40%.

iron-deficiency.short: Too little iron in the body's stores. It can exist before anaemia, while haemoglobin is still normal (iron deficiency without anaemia).

ferritin.short: The protein that stores iron. Its level in the blood (serum ferritin) is the usual first test of the body's iron stores.

vitamin-d.short: A vitamin made mostly in the skin from sunlight. Needed for bone, and involved in muscle and immunity. Measured in blood as 25(OH)D, in nmol·L⁻¹.

antioxidant.short: A substance that neutralises reactive oxygen species, e.g. vitamins C and E. The body makes its own; pills add large extra doses.
